assessment_summary: The proof is flawed in step 0024. The author attempts to reduce the 3-colourability of $G$ to the 3-colourability of its two components: the interior arrangement graph $\\overline{G}$ and the boundary cycle $\\partial G$. However, the chromatic number of a graph whose vertices are partitioned into two sets is not bounded by the maximum of the chromatic numbers of the induced subgraphs (it is bounded by their sum). A simple counterexample like $K_4$ partitioned into two edges shows that two 2-colourable subgraphs can form a 4-chromatic graph when edges between the parts are considered. The author themselves noted this exact logical failure in the update at the beginning of the post (line 0001).
counterexample: The author claims in step 0024 that since the interior subgraph $\\overline{G}$ is 3-colourable, showing that the boundary subgraph $\\partial G$ is 3-colourable is sufficient to prove that the entire graph $G$ is 3-colourable. This relies on the false premise that if the vertices of a graph can be partitioned into two sets which induce $\\le 3$-colourable subgraphs, the whole graph is $\\le 3$-colourable. This logic ignores the edges connecting the two parts, which constrain the colorings.\n\nA concrete counterexample to this logical deduction: Let $H$ be the complete graph $K_4$ with vertices $V = \\{1, 2, 3, 4\\}$. Partition the vertices into two sets $V_1 = \\{1, 2\\}$ and $V_2 = \\{3, 4\\}$. The induced subgraph $H[V_1]$ is a single edge, so $\\chi(H[V_1]) = 2 \\le 3$. The induced subgraph $H[V_2]$ is also a single edge, so $\\chi(H[V_2]) = 2 \\le 3$. Both parts are strictly $\\le 3$-colourable, but the entire graph $H = K_4$ requires 4 colours ($\\chi(H) = 4 > 3$). Therefore, independently bounding the chromatic numbers of $\\overline{G}$ and $\\partial G$ by 3 is not sufficient to bound $\\chi(G)$ by 3.
